A systems atlas of American democracy and the economy

Policy that favors insiders adds to the wealth that funds political spending.

You feel it at the kitchen table first. Rent climbs faster than pay. The people we elect often seem to hear someone else before they hear us. This atlas traces how that happens, one documented connection at a time.

Democracy

Who do they answer to?

Whether the people we elect have to face the voters who hired them, or can keep their jobs by pleasing a narrower crowd.

The economy

Who does our country work for?

How much of what working households produce and spend comes back to them as security, and how much collects at the top.

The whole system on one page

The map below follows the story across five areas, read from left to right. Concentrated wealth and market power decide who gets heard in politics. Officials in safe seats have less reason to listen to anyone else, and the checks inside government weaken when few of them face a real race. Policy then tilts toward insiders. Along the bottom, the return line carries that tilt back into wealth at the top, and the circle turns again.

How to read the map. Each card is one part, with every variable in it. Each arrow bundles the connections from one part to another, and its number counts them. The bright route is the main circuit. Choose any name or arrow for the detail.

PartCElectoral competition · Whether voters can fire them

Elections: who picks them?

Accountability depends on a real chance of losing. In most districts the general election is easy to predict, so the contest that decides the seat is a low-turnout primary. Incumbents also help write the rules for their own races, from district maps to voting procedures. When few officials face a competitive race, the pressure to serve the whole electorate fades.

The five variables

Each name is a condition that can rise or fall. The bold line says what a higher value means.

  • VariableC1

    Seats with little electoral competition

    Districts where one party wins by a wide margin, so its candidates face little risk in the general election. The model counts seats won by more than 10 percentage points.

    A higher value means more seats are safe for one party.

    3 in · 2 out

    Loops: R10, R12, R4a

  • VariableC2

    How often the primary decides the winner

    The share of seats where the general election is so predictable that the primary settles who takes office. Turnout in that deciding contest can be far lower than in November.

    A higher value means more seats are settled in the primary.

    1 in · 2 out

    Loops: R10

  • VariableC3

    Risk of losing office

    The credible threat that an incumbent will lose the next election. Where seats are competitive, the threat pushes officials to respond to voters before anyone is removed.

    A higher value means incumbents face a more credible chance of defeat.

    4 in · 4 out

    Loops: B4, R10, R11, R16

  • VariableC4

    Officeholders' control over election rules

    The power of people already in office to set district maps, voting-access rules and local election choices. This is rule-setting authority, and each rule's effect needs its own evidence.

    A higher value means incumbents have more say over the rules of their own elections.

    4 in · 3 out

    Loops: R10, R12, R4a, R4b

  • VariableC5

    Incumbents defeated or pushed into retirement

    Officeholders who lose an election or retire under threat of defeat. This consequence is measured separately from the pressure they face while still in office.

    A higher value means more incumbents lose or retire under threat of defeat in an election cycle.

    1 in · 1 out

    Loops: B4

LoopR10Reinforcing, feeds itself · lives in Elections

Safe-seat loop

Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates.

In a safe seat, the primary decides who wins, and few people vote in it. With little threat in November, officeholders answer to that smaller electorate and face less pressure from the wider public. Officials who cannot easily be removed can then write election rules that keep seats safe.

Read it aloud

More safe seats, more seats settled in the primary, less risk of losing office, more incumbents control election rules, and back to more safe seats.

Built from the signs: start with more, flip at each minus. A plus sign means the two move the same way. It does not mean the change is good.

Choose a box or an arrow to read it. Arrow keys move around the loop.

Red marks where R-01, all-party primaries with ranked general elections, acts: on L25, L08, C2. Choose another reform below to move the red to its targets.

The loop in V7's words

Seats with little electoral competition raise how often the primary decides the winner, which lowers the risk of losing office; lower risk raises officeholders' control over election rules, which raises the number of seats with little electoral competition.

Follow one turn

Start at C1, Safe seats, and suppose it rises. Press Play, or Next step to follow one numbered connection at a time.

  1. L08, Safe seats make the primary decisive. More safe seats means more seats settled in the primary. Sign +, same way; documented; under 2 years.
  2. L25, Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure. More seats settled in the primary means less risk of losing office. Sign −, opposite way; well supported; under 2 years.
  3. L53, Officials safe from defeat write rules for themselves. Less risk of losing office means more incumbents control election rules. Sign −, opposite way; plausible; 2 to 10 years.
  4. L42, Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats. More incumbents control election rules means more safe seats. Sign +, same way; documented; 2 to 10 years.

How sure, and how slow

The weakest step

L53, Officials safe from defeat write rules for themselves, is graded plausible: some evidence. The evidence is events, chiefly the 2025 mid-decade redistricting in states with one-party control, and legal analysis (Hasen 2020); no study measures this link directly.

The evidence

L08: Safe seats make the primary decisive and L42: Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats are documented, and L25: Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure is well supported. The weakest step is L53: Officials safe from defeat write rules for themselves, graded plausible: its evidence is the 2025 mid-decade redistricting in states with one-party control and legal analysis. Whether primaries make legislators more extreme is a separate, contested question, and the strongest tests found no effect.

The timing

One turn takes 2 to 10 years. L08: under 2 years. L25: under 2 years. L53: 2 to 10 years. L42: 2 to 10 years. Running up. V7 tracks it by the share of House seats settled in primaries, 2012 to 2024.

Closed: every step is a numbered connection.

Keep in mind

The qualification

Seat safety also comes from where voters live, and the claim that primary reform makes legislators more moderate is contested, so the loop concerns accountability more than ideology.

Where it shows up

Alaska's top-four primary with ranked-choice general elections survived a 2024 repeal measure by 743 votes out of 321,203 after a December 2024 recount. A second repeal is on the November 3, 2026 ballot, combined with repeal of the state's rule requiring disclosure of the true source of political donations. One election cycle is too short to show the design's long-run effect on accountability.

Where it bends

A seat becomes 'safe' above about a 10-point margin; Unite America, using Cook ratings rather than a margin threshold, counts 87% of House seats as effectively decided in the 2024 primaries and 88% in 2026.

How people adapt

Parties coordinate candidates under top-four (Alaska 2024); repeal campaigns; state preemption of local reform.

What would widen the deciding electorate

Widen the deciding electorate: top-four with ranked general (Alaska) or a single all-party primary (California, Washington); commissions for fairness; multi-member districts for competition. Drop the moderation claim.

ReformR-01Band: rules

All-party primaries with ranked general elections

Every voter, whatever their party, could vote in one first-round election, and two or more candidates would advance to a November ballot that all voters use. In seats that one party usually wins, the choice now made in a low-turnout party primary would move to the full electorate. In Massachusetts, unenrolled voters already pick one party's ballot. Under Question 3, every voter would see all candidates on one primary ballot from 2028. The Atlas takes no position on Question 3 or Ballot Measure 2.

Status, checked October 15, 2026

As of October 15, 2026, two measures on the November 3, 2026 ballot would change how primaries work. Alaska's Ballot Measure 2 (petition 24ESEG) would repeal the state's top-four primary and ranked-choice general election and return to party primaries. Massachusetts voters decide Question 3, which would replace party primaries for state and congressional offices with one primary listing every candidate, the top two advancing to November; if approved, it takes effect January 1, 2028. Nineteen states prohibit ranked-choice voting in some or all elections, by the National Conference of State Legislatures' count.

Result of the check: updated.

Disclosure. Oath & Action's editor works with the Yes on 3 campaign for Massachusetts Question 3 and promotes it through Veterans for All Voters, where he is Massachusetts state lead. He also co-leads Ranked Choice Melrose, a local campaign.

The problem it answers

Evidence for the problem: Plausible, some evidence

Cook Political Report rated 398 of 435 House seats safe for 2026, as reported by Unite America, an advocacy organization that funds primary-reform campaigns. Unite America's own count puts 383 seats (88%) as effectively decided in the 2026 primaries, which drew about 22.7 million voters, 9.4% of eligible voters. Both counts rest on ratings, which are forecasts, and on the group's definition of a safe seat.

Issues it aims at

  • DocumentedReformR-01I026
  • Well supportedReformR-01 ReformR-04 ReformR-03X01

What it changes, and where it acts

In a safe seat the general election is predictable, so the party primary picks the winner (L08: Safe seats make the primary decisive). That weakens the threat incumbents face from the wider public (L25: Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure). An all-party primary sends more than one candidate to November, which aims to lower C2: How often the primary decides the winner and raise C3: Risk of losing office. A top-two design advances two candidates; a top-four design advances four and can be paired with a ranked-choice general election. The reform sits on loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates), loop B4 (Electoral consequences can improve public performance) and loop R11 (Party loyalty weakens consequences for breaking norms).

Who could adopt it

States set nomination rules for state and federal offices.

  • State ballot

    Voters in initiative states

    Feasibility: medium. The route is open in some places, and a credible campaign could carry the reform through it by 2030.

    Massachusetts Question 3 and Alaska Ballot Measure 2, which would repeal Alaska's top-four primary and ranked-choice general election, are both on the November 3, 2026 ballot.

    Checked October 15, 2026

  • State statute

    Legislatures

    Feasibility: low. The route exists, but it needs a coalition that does not exist now.

    Legislators elected under the current rules rarely change them.

    No check date in V7

  • Local

    Home-rule cities, for municipal offices

    Feasibility: medium. The route is open in some places, and a credible campaign could carry the reform through it by 2030.

    This route is closed to cities and counties in the 19 states that prohibit ranked-choice voting in some or all elections, as of October 15, 2026.

    Checked October 15, 2026

  • Federal statute

    Congress under the Elections Clause

    Feasibility: very low. It needs a supermajority, a constitutional change or a reversal of court doctrine.

    No check date in V7

Who decides

States set nomination rules for state and federal offices. Where a state allows citizen initiatives, voters can change those rules at the ballot box, a route rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; Massachusetts Question 3 and Alaska's repeal measure are both on the November 3, 2026 ballot. Legislatures can act by statute, rated low because legislators elected under the current rules rarely change them. Home-rule cities can adopt the approach for municipal offices (medium) unless state law bans ranked ballots. Congress could act for federal races under the Elections Clause of the Constitution, which gets the lowest feasibility rating because most bills need 60 Senate votes while the filibuster stands (R-12).

Legal authority

States control primary rules within limits the Supreme Court has set. In Jones (2000) the Court barred blanket primaries that force parties to accept nominees chosen by all voters. In Washington State Grange (2008) it upheld a top-two primary that does not name party nominees. A ranked general election also requires a state with no ban on ranked ballots.

The evidence, graded twice

The problem and the remedy carry separate grades.

Problem

Plausible

Some evidence. The record for the problem is set out at the top of this page, under the problem it answers.

Remedy

Contested

Evidence disputed. More contested general elections and more candidates entering races are plausible results. Whether legislators become more moderate is contested: a 2014 study of state legislators by McGhee and colleagues found that more open primaries had little consistent effect on ideology, and experimental work finds that primary effects depend on conditions. Main limitation: Alaska's top-four system has a short record, so there is no long-run U.S. test of a top-four primary paired with a ranked general election.

Tradeoffs and how it could fail

Tradeoffs

Parties lose control over who carries their label, and some voters lose a party ballot line they value. Ranked tabulation takes longer to count. When two candidates from the same party advance, voters from the other party have no nominee of their own in November.

Costs

Implementation is a small one-time cost for state and county election offices. In Massachusetts, Question 3 would take effect January 1, 2028, leaving time to prepare. Party leaders and incumbents who are secure in their primaries lose influence, first as a threat and in practice at the next open seat.

Other options

Open partisan primaries let voters outside a party choose that party's ballot. Fusion voting (R-47) is another option, and proportional House districts (R-03) change the general election and leave the primary as it is. Two options are set aside as rejected. Blanket primaries are unconstitutional under Jones (2000). Turnout drives in closed-primary states raise participation and leave the rules on who may vote in a primary as they are.

How it could fail

Party organizations in both major parties and incumbents secure in their primaries are expected to resist. Parties can coordinate so that only one of their candidates competes; in Alaska in 2024 one candidate withdrew after the top-four primary, with party consultants citing the risk of splitting the vote. Voters or legislatures can reverse the rule, and nineteen states ban ranked-choice voting in some or all elections. The reform can also fall short if turnout stays low in the deciding round, or if voters misread the ballot and trust in results drops.

Carrying it out

Supporters first draft a measure and qualify it for the ballot, or a legislature passes a bill. A campaign follows. Before the first election under the new rules, election offices teach voters how the ballot works. After two election cycles, results can be judged by turnout in the round that decides each seat and by the number of contested general elections.

How to judge results

  • Share of seats with a competitive general election
  • Turnout in the round that decides each seat
  • Share of incumbents facing a credible general-election challenger
  • Voter understanding of the ballot, measured in exit surveys
  • Legislators' voting ideology, reported as exploratory because the best existing tests found no effect

The loop catalog

18 of the 23 loops feed themselves. 22 have a reform aimed at them.

A loop is a chain of causes that comes back to where it started. Each card draws one as boxes and arrows: follow the arrows around, and read each step with its word, raises or lowers. Improvement or decline can reinforce itself.

How to read a loop

  • raises: a plus sign. The two move the same way, which is not the same as good.
  • lowers: a minus sign. The two move in opposite ways.
  • Solid: documented or well supported. Ticks count the wait: one, under 2 years; two, 2 to 10; three, over 10.
  • Dashed: plausible, some evidence.
  • Dash and dot: contested, evidence disputed.
  • Dotted: hypothesis, untested.
  • Hollow: a sketched step with no numbered connection.

The shared language

Every line says what happens next, and how sure we are.

Each name on the map is a variable: a quantity or condition in the model that can rise or fall. Its definition states what a higher or lower value means. Each arrow is a connection: a claimed relationship between two variables. Its record explains the mechanism, gives the evidence grade and states the delay. Connection IDs begin with L, LE, LT, LX or T.

How to read a loop

  • raises: a plus sign. The two move the same way, which is not the same as good.
  • lowers: a minus sign. The two move in opposite ways.
  • Solid: documented or well supported. Ticks count the wait: one, under 2 years; two, 2 to 10; three, over 10.
  • Dashed: plausible, some evidence.
  • Dash and dot: contested, evidence disputed.
  • Dotted: hypothesis, untested.
  • Hollow: a sketched step with no numbered connection.
The full key

1 of 5

The tip is the effect

Read every arrow from its tail to its tip: the tail changes, and the tip moves. The tag on the line says which way.

  • Raises. The connected variables tend to move in the same direction, with the model's other conditions held steady. A positive sign does not mean a benefit.

  • Lowers. The connected variables tend to move in opposite directions, with the model's other conditions held steady.

  • Decides. A connection showing that one body holds legal power over something: it appoints, appropriates, preempts, enforces or sets a rate. It says who decides, without saying which way the decision goes, so it has no sign and never closes a loop.

2 of 5

Texture is the evidence

The line itself carries the evidence grade, so it survives a black-and-white print.

  • Documented: on the public record. The confidence label for a fact or event on the public record: a statute, a court ruling or an official statistic. It establishes the event; it says nothing about the size of an effect unless the record does.

  • Well supported: strong research evidence. The confidence label for a relationship on which several credible studies, designed to rule out other explanations, agree about direction. Each study's setting and limits still apply.

  • Plausible: some evidence. The confidence label for a coherent mechanism with some supporting evidence, where the studies are weak or few.

  • Contested: evidence disputed. The confidence label for a relationship on which credible studies disagree. Both sides are shown with the connection.

  • Hypothesis: untested. The confidence label for a proposed relationship that needs stronger evidence. Diagrams draw it as a dotted line, and it never serves as the only support for a claim.

  • Hollow: a sketched step. Three loops have steps that are not numbered connections. A complete path of connections that returns to the starting variable. If any closing step is only a hypothesis, the whole loop stays uncertain.

3 of 5

Ticks count the wait

The time between a change and its effect. Codes: S, under 2 years; M, 2 to 10 years; L, over 10 years.

  • One tick: under 2 years.

  • Two ticks: 2 to 10 years.

  • Three ticks: over 10 years.

4 of 5

Loops have a character

A loop is a chain of causes that comes back to where it started.

Reinforcing: feeds itself

A feedback loop whose returning effect amplifies the first change. Improvement or decline can reinforce itself.

18 of the 23 loops reinforce. Count the minus signs around a loop: an even number, or none, makes it reinforcing.

Balancing: pushes back

A feedback loop whose response pushes back against the first change. How well it works depends on whether each corrective step can act.

5 balance. An odd number of minus signs makes a loop push back.

A chain of causes that returns to its starting variable. Reinforcing loops amplify change and balancing loops counteract it; either kind can produce good or harmful results.

5 of 5

Color is the layer

In the Night Edition, color marks attention, and the letter marks the layer.

  • Newsprint: the route you are reading. On the overview it is the main circuit, from Wealth to Policy and back.

  • Gray: context. The other large flows between parts.

  • Red: where a reform acts. One job per view. Red never marks a sign, a grade, a party or harm.

The layer is the letter and the place. The core parts, A to E, run across the middle in the order the story moves. Outside forces, X, sit above. Your household, EC, and technology, TC, sit below. On this dark ground, hue keeps one job, and the letter carries the layer.

14 common mix-ups

Questions readers ask, with the answer the map supports and the misreading to avoid.

  • A district where the incumbent could lose but never does: is that pressure, sanction, both or neither?

    Pressure without sanction. Risk of losing office can be present while incumbents defeated stays at zero; the accountability loop needs both.

    The mix-up: Treating any competitive-looking seat as accountable.

  • In one or two sentences, explain how a zoning meeting can change rents across a city.

    Owners whose equity rises with scarcity attend and block new homes; fewer homes keep rents high.

    The mix-up: Rents rise only because landlords are greedy, or only because of interest rates.

  • Does housing scarcity raise the top 1% share of wealth?

    Not in the atlas. Scarcity widens the owner-renter gap; when house prices outrun stocks the top 1% share tends to fall.

    The mix-up: Equating every wealth gap with the top 1%.

  • The 43-day shutdown happened. What part of the trust-through-service loop does that prove?

    That service failed (an event on quality of public services). It does not show that the failure lowered trust, or that trust lowered funding; those links carry their own grades.

    The mix-up: A vivid case proves a whole loop.

  • Where does a rule allowing homes by right enter the atlas?

    At the link “Owners' equity drives opposition to new housing”, where owners with equity resist new homes, and at housing scarcity.

    The mix-up: Reforms act on outcomes directly.

  • Name one reform a state can adopt without Congress, and one that needs sixty Senate votes today.

    Examples: on-cycle local elections (state statute); proportional House districts (federal statute).

    The mix-up: Every reform waits on Washington.

  • A line labelled auth, with no plus or minus sign, connects Congress to public investment. What does it mean?

    Authority: Congress has the power to decide; the line does not say which way it will.

    The mix-up: Every line is a cause.

  • Why does the atlas not give each reform a single score?

    The four outcome families use different units, some reforms help one and cost another, and the evidence differs in quality.

    The mix-up: More plus signs means a better reform.

  • What did the largest feed experiments find about polarization?

    Changing the feed changed what people saw a great deal and their partisan hostility little or not at all.

    The mix-up: Algorithms caused polarization, settled.

  • Household income rose last year. Does that mean household wealth rose too?

    Not necessarily. Income is a flow; wealth is a stock that also moves with asset prices and debts.

    The mix-up: Stock-flow confusion (Sweeney and Sterman).

  • The same house-price rise: who gains most, a renter under 35 or an owner over 55?

    The owner; ownership and equity differ sharply by age.

    The mix-up: Averages describe every household.

  • Pick one reform profile. Which office decides it, and how could you reach that office?

    It depends on the route. The route board on this page lists who acts on each route for every profile.

    The mix-up: No one decides; it just happens.

  • Name one thing that decides how a productivity gain is split between pay and profit.

    Bargaining power, which the rules for organizing shape. Productivity growth raises what can be paid; it does not settle who gets it.

    The mix-up: Pay tracks productivity automatically, or pay never responds to it.

  • Which office sets your electric rates?

    For an investor-owned utility, the state public utility commission. For public power or a co-op, a city council or co-op board. In PJM states the grid operator's capacity auction, overseen by federal regulators, also feeds into bills.

    The mix-up: The power company sets its own prices, or Washington sets them.
